title: Markandeya inside the child
hookLine: a sage swims the flood and finds the whole world inside a child
carry: all unfolds from the one and folds back
tomorrow: a mountain grows to block the sun. what made it bow?
last: A WHOLE DIAGRAM IN ONE SHORT WORD.

lines: A CHILD ON A BANYAN LEAF.
THE WORLD, BREATHED IN AND OUT.
cards: The sage Markandeya asks to see the Lord's power, and the vision comes. The world goes under a flood: no shore, no sun, only water and dark wind. He swims alone for what feels like ages.
Then, on a banyan branch above the waves, he sees a small child lying on a leaf, glowing, his toe in his mouth. As Markandeya comes close, the child breathes in, and the sage is drawn inside him.
There he sees the whole world again: mountains, rivers, cities, even his own hermitage. Then the child breathes out, and he's back in the flood. In the Bhagavata Purana, the child is Vishnu.
So: where does everything come from, and where does it go back to?

teach.b: Hindu teaching pictures the world in great cycles: it unfolds, and in time it folds back into the one it came from, pralaya, and later unfolds again. Markandeya saw both in a single breath.
The Sri Yantra is read the same two ways. Outward from the bindu, where Shiva and Shakti are one: triangles open into triangles, then petals, then rings, out to the square, the world as it's lived.
Inward from the square, layer by layer: that's samhara, folding back, the many returning to the one. Not grim; a homecoming. The worship from two days ago walks that road.
A neighbor tradition says something close.

teach.h: THE QUR'AN: UNTO HIM WE RETURN.
teach.b: The Qur'an describes the patient, who say, when misfortune strikes them: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning."

What the two share: everything comes from one source and goes back to it, and the going back is a homecoming, not a void. The honest difference: in the Qur'an, God is the Creator, and creation stays distinct from God.

teach.h: ALL UNFOLDS FROM THE ONE, AND FOLDS BACK.
teach.b: In Sri Vidya's reading, the layers unfold from the Goddess as her own expression, and the return is the many folding back into the one.

how: Sri Vidya teachers describe the Sri Yantra in two orders: srishti, outward from the bindu, and samhara, inward from the outer square, the order the worship follows; Hindu teaching pictures the world unfolding and returning in great cycles. Muslims know the words of Qur'an 2:156, said when misfortune or a loss comes.

a world that unfolds from the One and folds back into it

games.q: out and back — tap the pairs.
p: saw the world inside a child

s: inside the child, Markandeya found the world gone for good
he found it whole, mountains, rivers, his own hermitage, breathed in and out.
Sri Vidya teachers read the yantra both outward and inward
outward as creation, srishti; inward as the way back, samhara.
the Qur'an and Sri Vidya picture the return in the same way
both speak of a return; the Qur'an keeps Creator and creation distinct, while Sri Vidya reads the layers as the Goddess's own unfolding.

games.q: a friend whose grandfather died this year asks whether 'returning' is only a sad word. what do both texts you heard today offer?
o: a homecoming: in the Qur'an, a return to God; in Sri Vidya, the many folding back to the one.
an ending with nothing after it; both texts treat the return as a loss.
a reversal that cancels out the life that came before it.
games.why: both speak of everything coming from one source and going back to it. they picture it differently, and neither calls the return a void.

practice: Close your eyes. On each in-breath, picture the yantra's layers folding gently inward toward the point; on each out-breath, picture them opening back out to the square.
Let the breath set the pace, and when the picture fades, just keep the breathing.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Yantra, read two ways: srishti, unfolding out from the point, and samhara, folding back to it.

orig.note: Sanskrit srishti, creation, sending forth: the yantra read outward from the point.

carryVoice: Last line for today: all unfolds from the One and folds back. Markandeya saw it in one breath. Day sixteen thirty-seven.
